name: Dana Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in lettings at Harbour Lane Property, an agency in a seaside town that does long lets for families and holiday lets in summer. My day starts with the overnight messages from holiday guests, then I'm out doing check-ins, inspections and the odd viewing. I know most of the landlords personally, a lot of them from church or the school gate. I love the town and the people. What wears me out is August, when every guest wants a cot and nobody can work the hot tub.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. Our manager brought in a tool that drafts replies to holiday guests, and after a few weeks of everyone else using it I did too. It's handy for 'where's the parking' messages. I'm a steady agent, middle of the road, but landlords trust me because I turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped but handy for the small stuff. At work I'd say keep the guest tool, it saves time. Online I'd probably not say anything, maybe share a joke in the church group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased. My job's secure, my husband Rui's plumbing business is busy, and we've got our little terrace with a fair bit saved. We're hoping to start a family in a couple of years, so steady suits us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing the job and keep saving, about five hundred a month. Maybe take a property management qualification so I can step up to lettings manager. Rui and I might do up the back bedroom for a nursery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. Grateful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your work that worries you in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The seasons. Holiday lets can have a bad summer if the weather's poor or people stay away, and our pay has a bonus on bookings. Two summers ago holiday bookings dropped a fifth and my bonus went with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you cope then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We tightened up, Rui did extra weekend jobs. It wasn't a disaster because we had savings. That's why I'm careful.

I'd tell work to **keep the guest tool**, as it saves time.
think: I'd be **pleased** that my job is secure.
Steady suits us as we hope to **start a family**.
do: Take a **property management** qualification to step up.
Do up the **back bedroom** for a future nursery.

fieldNote: Her standing worry is **seasonal bookings**, not AI.
She values **savings** because of a past bad summer.
She adopts tools **after others** try them, as expected.

steps.text: Take a property management qualification for lettings manager
Decorate the back bedroom as a future nursery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and we'll adapt. At work I'd say let's use it for guest messages and bookings and keep the personal side. To friends at church I'd say it's not the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think a lot of my desk work goes. The guest messages, bookings and checking, that's what the card says. But check-ins, inspections and sorting out a broken boiler at ten at night stay, so I'd still have a job, maybe with fewer hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever booking system Harbour Lane brings in, once the others had shown me it works. I'd keep saving and maybe hold off the nursery a few months to see how hours go. I'd ask my manager about taking on more of the long-let inspections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's probably fine, but my hours might drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fewer hours would mean what for your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less of my bonus, maybe a day less a week. Rui's business would cover us. It would just push the baby plans back a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should help people whose hours drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Families and churches first, honestly. I don't want to rely on government. If a business can save money, people should look for new work, not wait for a handout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's scary but we'll get through it as a town. At work I'd ask the manager what happens to us. To the church group I'd say we need to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Harbour Lane needs one or two people instead of six. A system that does all the guest messages, bookings, pricing and paperwork by 2028 leaves only the keys and inspections. My job shrinks to part-time at best until the robots, around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Rui about me helping run his plumbing business, the bookings and quotes side, since plumbers will be needed for a while. I'd also think about starting my own tiny lettings service for landlords I know, using the AI tools to do the admin. And we'd keep every penny saved until we knew where we stood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd worry about the baby plans, and about the town. But I'd feel I could do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd start your own lettings service. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know about twenty landlords who'd trust me over a computer. With the AI doing the admin, I could look after their homes on my own, charging less than Harbour Lane. Rui says I'd be good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the three-year gap before robots change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me until about 2031 where people still need someone to turn up with keys and check a property. That's my window. After that, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we start now. At work I'd suggest we plan. At church I'd say we'll manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have time to set up my own lettings service before it hits. And maybe have a baby before things get rough. That's a lot to fit in, but it's possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the lettings service slowly in year one, with a few landlords, alongside Harbour Lane. I'd use the AI tools every day to learn them. Rui and I would try for a baby next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Busy and a bit nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a baby sooner rather than later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because later looks harder. If jobs are tight in 2031, I'd rather have a toddler than be pregnant. Rui agrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave Harbour Lane?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably by year three. I'd want enough landlords first. I wouldn't leave without a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty and we should plan calmly. At work I'd say let's change step by step. At church I'd say there's no point panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I'd have time for a family, a new business and learning the tools. I'd be 37 when it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Harbour Lane, go for lettings manager, and have a baby in a couple of years. I'd start my own lettings service in five years or so. Rui and I might buy a small holiday let ourselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buy a holiday let? Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People will still want seaside holidays, AI or not. And it's something we own that earns. My parents always said own something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk in waiting five years for the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I'd watch the office. If they stop hiring for summer, I'd move sooner. I'll know.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit just when we want a baby. What would help is easy rules for setting up small businesses, and local training through the council or college. Not handouts, just a way to work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the town. If agencies and shops cut staff, the young people leave. Then the church, the school and everything else gets smaller.

headlineQuote: If agencies and shops cut staff, the young people leave. Then the church, the school and everything else gets smaller.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old lettings agent** in a seaside town, handling long lets and holiday lets.
She is married to **Rui**, who runs a plumbing business, and they hope to start a family.
She uses AI **now and then**, after others prove it, and values church and community.
In fast AGI she plans **her own lettings service**, while slower versions let her put family first.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028**, arriving just as they hope to have a baby.
whatWouldHelp: She wants easy **small-business rules** and **local training**, not handouts.
